Pi Server

I wanted one page that could tell me whether anything at home was broken. It became a full monitoring and control stack running as a system service on a Raspberry Pi 5.

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • WebSockets
  • SQLite
  • Linux
  • systemd

Gallery

What It Does

A single-page control panel for my home network. It shows live hardware stats for the Pi and my desktop, an inventory of everything connected, the status of the services I self-host, and controls for the things I'd otherwise have to walk across the house to do.

The brief I gave myself was narrow: everything I want to know should be visible without clicking, and everything I want to do should be one button. Every feature since has had to earn its place against that.

Key Features

  • Live system stats. CPU, memory, temperature, disk and uptime for the Pi, streamed over a WebSocket rather than polled, so the numbers move in real time instead of stepping.
  • Desktop monitoring. A companion agent on my Windows PC reports CPU, memory, disk and GPU telemetry back to the dashboard, with GPU stats read from NVIDIA's management library directly.
  • Remote power control. Wake-on-LAN to start the PC, plus a queued command channel for sleep and shutdown, so a control issued while the PC is off isn't lost.
  • Network scanning. Regular scans discover what's connected. Results are stored with history, and devices can be searched, sorted, tagged, renamed, annotated or marked reviewed.
  • Ad blocking. Integrates with the Pi-hole API rather than reimplementing it, surfacing query and blocking stats alongside everything else.
  • Connectivity. Latency polling, on-demand speed tests, and a VPN status panel with a restart control for when the mesh network gets stuck.
  • Push alerts. Threshold and service-health alerts delivered to my phone, so I find out something's wrong without having the dashboard open.

How It Works

Backend

Python and FastAPI. Stats that change constantly go out over WebSockets; everything else is a plain REST endpoint. Device history and scan results live in SQLite. Network discovery shells out to nmap and parses the results. External integrations — the ad blocker's REST API, the VPN's status output, the push notification service — are each wrapped behind a small module, so a change on their side touches one file.

Frontend

Hand-written HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework. The layout is a four-region shell: a permanent left navigation sidebar moving from the overview down through each subsystem, a top bar with labelled status dots for at-a-glance health, a card grid as the main content area, and a right sidebar on the overview holding a merged Pi-and-PC stats card. Adding a page means adding a nav entry and a content module, nothing else.

Config that survives its own updates

Early on, updating the dashboard meant replacing the application directory — which also wiped the credentials and settings stored inside it. Now every piece of persistent state lives in a separate config directory outside the application tree. Updating is a directory swap with nothing to back up first.

Commands for a machine that isn't listening

Sleep and shutdown can't be pushed to a PC that's asleep, and Wake-on-LAN is fire-and-forget with no acknowledgement. Rather than making the dashboard talk to the PC synchronously, controls write to a command queue that the agent drains on its own schedule. The dashboard records intent; delivery is the agent's problem.

Deployment

The dashboard runs as a systemd service, so it starts on boot and restarts itself if it crashes. The PC agent starts automatically through Windows Task Scheduler under a dedicated local account. A direct Ethernet link between the Pi and the desktop gives Wake-on-LAN a reliable path that doesn't depend on Wi-Fi.
